questions.question: The six Fundamental Rights
questions.imageAlt: Six boxes showing the groups of Fundamental Rights
questions.explanation:
Part III of the Constitution, Articles 12 to 35, protects your most basic freedoms. If one of these rights is violated, you can approach the courts.

There are six groups of rights: Equality, Freedom, Protection against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Constitutional Remedies. The Right to Property used to be a seventh, but it was removed in 1978.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India guarantees the Right to Life and Personal Liberty?
questions.mentorScolding: That is okay. The answer is Article 21. Every mistake helps you remember it better.
questions.explanation: Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, and nobody can be deprived of them except by a procedure established by law. The courts have read privacy, dignity and speedy trial into it. Article 19 holds the freedoms, Article 20 protects against unfair conviction, and Article 22 covers arrest and detention.

questions.question: The Right to Education was made a Fundamental Right (Article 21A) by which Constitutional Amendment?
questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is perfectly alright. It is 86th Amendment. You will get it next time.
questions.explanation: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6 to 14. The Right to Education Act, 2009 brought it into force on 1 April 2010. The 42nd Amendment added Fundamental Duties, and the 44th removed the right to property from Part III.

questions.question: Who described Article 32, the Right to Constitutional Remedies, as the heart and soul of the Constitution?
questions.mentorScolding: Gently now. The answer is Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. Take a breath, you are doing just fine.
questions.explanation: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution. It lets a citizen go straight to the Supreme Court to enforce a Fundamental Right, through the writs of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.

questions.question: Match each Article with the right it guarantees.

pairs.right: Protection of life and personal liberty

questions.mentorScolding: That is alright. The correct pairs are shown below. Take your time with them.
questions.explanation: Article 14 gives equality before law, Article 17 abolishes untouchability, Article 19(1)(a) protects freedom of speech and expression, and Article 21 protects life and personal liberty. These four are asked in almost every cycle.

questions.question: Article ___ abolishes untouchability.
questions.hint: The Right to Equality runs from Article 14 to Article 18.
questions.mentorScolding: No worries at all. 17 is the one. Learning takes patience, and you are showing it.
questions.explanation: Article 17 abolishes untouchability. The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 gives it teeth. It sits under the Right to Equality, Articles 14 to 18.

questions.question: The Right to Property was removed from Part III by the ___ Amendment.
questions.hint: It came in 1978, after the Emergency.
questions.mentorScolding: That is okay. The answer is 44th. Every mistake helps you remember it better.
questions.explanation: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed the right to property from Part III. It became a legal right under Article 300A.

questions.question: Look at the diagram. How many groups of Fundamental Rights does the Constitution guarantee today?
questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is perfectly alright. It is 6. You will get it next time.
questions.explanation: Today there are six groups: Equality, Freedom, Protection against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Constitutional Remedies. The Right to Property was a seventh until the 44th Amendment removed it.

questions.question: The right to life under Article 21 can never be suspended, even during a National Emergency.
questions.mentorScolding: Gently now. The answer is True. Take a breath, you are doing just fine.
questions.explanation: Since the 44th Amendment, 1978, the rights under Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended during a National Emergency. The other Fundamental Rights can be.

questions.question: The Right to Property is still a Fundamental Right.
questions.mentorScolding: No worries at all. False is the one. Learning takes patience, and you are showing it.
questions.explanation: The 44th Amendment, 1978 removed it from Part III. Today it is a legal right under Article 300A.

questions.question: Who runs the Union?
questions.imageAlt: Chart of the President, Vice President, Prime Minister with ministers, and Attorney General
questions.explanation:
The President is the head of State, and the executive power of the Union is formally vested in the President under Article 53.

In practice the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers run the government and advise the President under Article 74. The Vice President and the Attorney General complete the Union Executive.

questions.question: Who appoints the Prime Minister of India?
questions.mentorScolding: That is okay. The answer is The President. Every mistake helps you remember it better.
questions.explanation: Under Article 75(1) the President appoints the Prime Minister, in practice the leader of the party or coalition that commands a majority in the Lok Sabha. The other ministers are appointed on the Prime Minister's advice.

questions.question: Which Article vests the executive power of the Union in the President?
questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is perfectly alright. It is Article 53. You will get it next time.
questions.explanation: Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President, to be used directly or through officers under him. Article 52 only says there shall be a President, Article 74 creates the Council of Ministers to aid and advise him, and Article 75 deals with the ministers.

questions.question: What is the minimum age to be eligible for election as President of India?
questions.mentorScolding: Gently now. The answer is 35 years. Take a breath, you are doing just fine.
questions.explanation: A candidate for President must be an Indian citizen, at least 35 years old, and qualified to be elected to the Lok Sabha (Article 58). The Vice President also has to be at least 35.

questions.question: Match each Article with its subject.

pairs.right: There shall be a President of India
Council of Ministers to aid and advise

questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is okay. Have a calm look at the pairs below.
questions.explanation: Article 52 says there shall be a President, Article 53 vests the executive power in him, Article 74 creates the Council of Ministers to aid and advise him, and Article 76 provides for the Attorney General.

questions.question: The President of India is elected for a term of ___ years.
questions.mentorScolding: No worries at all. 5 is the one. Learning takes patience, and you are showing it.
questions.explanation: Article 56 gives the President a five-year term, counted from the day he enters office. He continues until his successor takes charge.

questions.question: The Prime Minister is appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
questions.mentorScolding: That is okay. The answer is False. Every mistake helps you remember it better.
questions.explanation: The President appoints the Prime Minister under Article 75(1). The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha but has no role in appointing the Prime Minister.

questions.question: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which Part of the Constitution?
questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is perfectly alright. It is Part IV. You will get it next time.
questions.explanation: The Directive Principles are in Part IV, Articles 36 to 51. They guide the State but cannot be enforced in court, and the idea comes from the Irish Constitution. Part III is Fundamental Rights and Part IV-A is Fundamental Duties.

questions.question: Which Article directs the State to secure a Uniform Civil Code for citizens?
questions.mentorScolding: Gently now. The answer is Article 44. Take a breath, you are doing just fine.
questions.explanation: Article 44 asks the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code for all citizens. Article 40 is about village panchayats, Article 48 about agriculture and animal husbandry, and Article 51 about international peace and security.

questions.question: Match each Article of Part IV with its directive.
questions.mentorScolding: That is alright. The correct pairs are shown below. Take your time with them.
questions.explanation: Article 40 asks the State to organise village panchayats, Article 44 aims at a Uniform Civil Code, Article 48 covers agriculture and animal husbandry, and Article 50 separates the judiciary from the executive.

questions.question: The Directive Principles of State Policy were borrowed from the ___ Constitution.
questions.mentorScolding: No worries at all. Irish is the one. Learning takes patience, and you are showing it.
questions.explanation: The Directive Principles come from the Irish Constitution. Fundamental Rights draw on the US Bill of Rights, and the parliamentary system on Britain.

questions.question: Directive Principles of State Policy can be enforced in a court of law.
questions.mentorScolding: That is okay. The answer is False. Every mistake helps you remember it better.
questions.explanation: Directive Principles are non-justiciable. They guide the State in making laws, but a court cannot enforce them, unlike Fundamental Rights.

questions.question: Who presides over a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament?
questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is perfectly alright. It is The Speaker of Lok Sabha. You will get it next time.
questions.explanation: Under Article 108 the President summons a joint sitting to settle a deadlock over an ordinary Bill, and the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over it. Joint sittings are rare. The standard examples are the Dowry Prohibition Bill 1961, the Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill 1978 and the POTA Bill 2002.

questions.question: What is the maximum permissible gap between two sessions of Parliament?
questions.mentorScolding: Gently now. The answer is Six months. Take a breath, you are doing just fine.
questions.explanation: Article 85 says that six months must not pass between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next. That is why Parliament has to meet at least twice a year.

questions.question: Match each Article with what it deals with.
questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is okay. Have a calm look at the pairs below.
questions.explanation: Article 108 provides for a joint sitting, Article 110 defines a Money Bill, Article 112 requires the Annual Financial Statement, and Article 123 lets the President issue ordinances when Parliament is not in session.

questions.question: The Rajya Sabha has a maximum strength of ___ members.
questions.mentorScolding: No worries at all. 250 is the one. Learning takes patience, and you are showing it.
questions.explanation: Article 80 sets the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha at 250: up to 238 representatives of States and Union Territories, and 12 nominated members.

questions.question: The Rajya Sabha can be dissolved by the President.
questions.mentorScolding: That is okay. The answer is False. Every mistake helps you remember it better.
questions.explanation: The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is never dissolved. One third of its members retire every second year. Only the Lok Sabha can be dissolved.

questions.question: What is the retirement age of a Supreme Court judge?
questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is perfectly alright. It is 65 years. You will get it next time.
questions.explanation: Under Article 124(2) a Supreme Court judge holds office until 65. A High Court judge retires at 62 under Article 217.

questions.question: A High Court judge retires at the age of ___.
questions.mentorScolding: Gently now. The answer is 62. Take a breath, you are doing just fine.
questions.explanation: Under Article 217 a High Court judge holds office until the age of 62. For a Supreme Court judge the age is 65 under Article 124.

questions.question: Match each writ with its meaning.

pairs.right: Produce the detained person before the court
Command a public official to do their duty
Quash an order of a lower court
Question by what authority one holds public office

questions.mentorScolding: That is alright. The correct pairs are shown below. Take your time with them.
questions.explanation: Habeas corpus means "you may have the body", and it frees a person from illegal detention. Mandamus commands a public official to perform a duty. Certiorari quashes an order of a lower court. Quo warranto challenges a person’s right to hold a public office.

questions.question: Which Schedule of the Constitution contains the Union, State and Concurrent Lists?
questions.mentorScolding: No worries at all. Seventh Schedule is the one. Learning takes patience, and you are showing it.
questions.explanation: The Seventh Schedule divides powers between the Union and the States through three lists: Union, State and Concurrent. Residuary powers rest with the Union.

questions.question: The ___ Amendment introduced Panchayati Raj institutions as constitutional bodies.
questions.mentorScolding: That is okay. The answer is 73rd. Every mistake helps you remember it better.
questions.explanation: The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule on Panchayats. The 74th Amendment covers Municipalities through Part IX-A and the Twelfth Schedule.

questions.question: Match each Schedule with its subject.
questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is okay. Have a calm look at the pairs below.
questions.explanation: The Seventh Schedule holds the three legislative lists, the Eighth lists the recognised languages, the Tenth carries the anti-defection law, and the Twelfth lists the functions of Municipalities.

questions.question: Article 1 describes India as a Union of States.
questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is perfectly alright. It is True. You will get it next time.
questions.explanation: Article 1 says that India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. The word Union shows that no State has the right to secede.

questions.question: Which Article empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs to enforce Fundamental Rights?
questions.mentorScolding: Gently now. The answer is Article 32. Take a breath, you are doing just fine.
questions.explanation: Article 32 lets a person approach the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights. Article 226 gives High Courts a wider writ power.

questions.question: Article ___ directs the State to secure a Uniform Civil Code.
questions.mentorScolding: No worries at all. 44 is the one. Learning takes patience, and you are showing it.
questions.explanation: Article 44, in Part IV, directs the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code for all citizens.

questions.question: Who is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
questions.mentorScolding: That is okay. The answer is The Vice President. Every mistake helps you remember it better.
questions.explanation: Under Article 89 the Vice President of India is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

questions.question: How many Schedules does the Constitution of India currently have?
questions.mentorScolding: Not quite, and that is perfectly alright. It is 12. You will get it next time.
questions.explanation: The Constitution began with 8 Schedules and now has 12, after the Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh and Twelfth were added by amendments.

questions.question: The minimum age to become President of India is ___ years.
questions.mentorScolding: Gently now. The answer is 35. Take a breath, you are doing just fine.
questions.explanation: Under Article 58 a candidate for President must be at least 35 years old, a citizen of India and qualified to be a member of the Lok Sabha.

questions.question: Fundamental Rights are listed in Part IV of the Constitution.
questions.mentorScolding: No worries at all. False is the one. Learning takes patience, and you are showing it.
questions.explanation: Fundamental Rights are in Part III. Part IV holds the Directive Principles of State Policy.
